items.string: iLit is a litigation intelligence tool for immigration law that I have been building independently. It reads every Federal Court immigration file and decision, connects them, and answers the questions a litigation analyst is asked every week, with the source behind every answer. This is where it is today, and where it could go next.
Machine-drafted French preview; review by a fluent French speaker is required. Legal terminology is not final.
Status overview · shared informally with the CBSA Hearings and Litigation Division · 28 Sept 2026

this is not a request to adopt anything or start a pilot. The project runs on public data, outside government, and moves quickly because of it. The last section sets out an unofficial idea of what modest funding would speed up, in three sizes.
What changes when you go from CanLII to iLit
The Division has no Westlaw or Lexis. CanLII is free and reliable, but it only lets you find and read one decision at a time. Everything else is done by hand.

Buying a commercial platform would not close this gap either. A September 2026 scan found no Canadian product with Federal Court file tracking, Minister win/loss data or immigration citation trends. The tools that do this kind of analysis cover US courts only.
iLit uses public information only. It collects it, keeps the original untouched, reads it into facts, and connects the pieces.
Public sources are collected, read, linked, and turned into answers for analysts

It collects public court records, keeps the originals untouched, reads them into structured facts, connects them to each other, and answers the questions analysts ask. Every answer can be traced back to the original page.
Dockets, decisions and authorities are joined by file number and by citation
CanLII has only the middle box. iLit connects each decision to its court file and to everything it cites, so you can move from “what happened” to “why” to “on what authority” in a click.

It tracks every Federal Court file, not just the ones with decisions

Today, checking what has happened on a Federal Court immigration file means looking it up on the court’s website by hand, one case at a time. iLit already holds the docket history of every immigration file ever filed, 316,940 of them with 3.6 million entries, available instantly. It is designed to be refreshed so it stays accurate.

statistics can cover every case ever filed, not only the files JRU received. Most immigration files never produce a published decision (leave is usually refused without reasons, files are discontinued or settled), so tools built on decisions, CanLII included, never see them. One caveat: the docket is typed by Registry staff, so some entries contain errors, and any statistic inherits them.

Motion types are still a prototype, identified for about a quarter of files in a sample.
This layer began as a Python version of the JRU Personal Inventory Tool, an Excel workbook for tracking one person’s caseload. iLit keeps its logic and scales it to every file in the court.
On CanLII a citation is a link. In iLit each citation knows where it sits in the decision, which paragraph it points to, and how it is used across the whole library.
A citation in a decision becomes a link to the exact paragraph and then feeds analysis
Done for 1.44 million citations; pinpointed to the paragraph for 183,010 of them

Most tools stop at “this case cites that case”. iLit knows exactly where each citation sits, which paragraph it points to, and adds them up across the whole library to answer questions no single decision can.
Who cites it, how often, in which courts, and how the Minister fared in those cases. Click any year to read the passages.
Flags authorities as emerging, dominant or declining, and suggests possible successors: the kind of shift seen when Vavilov replaced Dunsmuir.
For a decision in the library, lists authorities that at least a fifth of its 40 closest peers cite but it doesn’t.
Finds cases that share rare authorities, which say more about similarity than sharing Vavilov does.
Follows chains of citations from the Supreme Court down through the Federal Court cases that relied on them.
Upload a Word or PDF memo. Citations and statute references in standard formats are found, matched and linked to their text. Nothing is saved.
AI gives every paragraph a meaning, and ties it to its authorities

Counting citations tells you what a court relied on. The next question is what each paragraph is doing: stating the issue, setting out the Minister’s position, applying a test, rejecting an argument. iLit uses rules and AI together to label each paragraph, then links it to the citations inside it.
Rules and AI label each paragraph, rules verify, and paragraphs are linked to citations

Each paragraph gets a meaning (what it is doing and what it is about) and is tied to the authorities cited in it. Done so far for about 93% of the paragraphs in 300 core decisions (13,424 paragraph records), with 6,260 citations linked to the paragraphs that use them.
changes the source text, citations or facts.

This means an analyst can ask “show me every paragraph where a court applied the mootness test, and what it cited” and get the answer across the core decisions at once. A test search for “mootness” returned 25 paragraphs (the display limit), 33 citations and 21 linked authorities.
The AI layer is an early prototype. It has been run on 300 core decisions using a low-cost public AI service, at roughly a tenth of a cent per decision, and only on public court decisions.
The same engine is designed to work on the Division’s own material

Everything iLit does to a court decision (finding its citations, splitting it into paragraphs, linking each citation to the case it names and the paragraph it points to) works on ordinary text. That is deliberate. The same reader can be pointed at draft submissions, precedent memos and briefing notes, and connect them to the whole body of public case law.
Today a public AI reads only public decisions; with local hardware the AI runs inside the department and can read internal documents

Today a low-cost public AI is used, and only on public decisions. iLit is being built so the same AI step can run on a local model inside the department. That opens live AI analysis of the Division’s own internal documents, which a public service can never be given.

It is designed to take in new cases as they happen
A research tool is only useful if it stays current. iLit was built from the start to add new decisions and new docket activity incrementally, not by rebuilding everything.
New court activity is checked, stored once, read and linked, then the file is scheduled for its next check
Each step is built and has been run. Today they are started by hand; joining them into one nightly run is a next step.
each file records when it was

iLit is built to take in new decisions and new docket activity as they appear, without redoing work: each step only handles what is new or changed, and can pick up where it left off after an interruption.

Every page is fingerprinted when stored, so duplicates are skipped. Processing steps such as indexing and tagging only handle items they haven’t done yet.
Picks up where it left off
Overnight processing can be stopped and resumed safely, with a lock so two runs never collide. Collectors pull only recent months and stop if a site asks for human verification.
Today each run is started by hand, and a few hand-offs are manual (loading collected decisions, linking their citations). Joining those up and running it nightly needs an always-on machine.
Why a litigation analyst would use it every week
“What’s the status of the Division’s open files?”
Every file’s docket history is already stored and searchable; a live lookup refreshes any single file in seconds.
Look up each file on the court’s website by hand and read the docket.
Look up each authority on CanLII, one by one.
Upload it. Every authority the rules recognise is found and linked, so its trend and track record are one click away.
“What does the Court do with s. 34(1)(f) right now?”
An old precedent memo, or days of reading.
The current leading, emerging and declining authorities, plus the cases the individual won.
“How much immigration litigation challenges CBSA decisions?”
Being tested: files sorted by who made the decision under challenge. A grouped view is still to build.
“Is a brief missing a case the Court usually expects?”
For decisions in the library today, a gap check against the 40 most similar ones. Running it on the Division’s own drafts is a next step.
“How does a draft compare with how courts handled these arguments?”
Each argument in the draft matched to how courts dealt with it, inside the department.
The original decision and docket are kept untouched. Core facts keep a pointer to the sentence or docket line they came from.
Core facts come from fixed rules that give the same answer every time. If something can’t be found, iLit says “not found”.
AI adds labels in a separate layer. It never changes the source, the citations or the facts, and its labels are automatically checked against the source.

Public sources only. The Federal Court collectors space out their requests and stop if the site asks for human verification.

What works today, and what I’m working on next

Everything above exists in code and runs today on my own workstation, except the items that depend on local AI or internal documents. Some of it is finished; some is a working prototype that needs checking against real use.

Judge-level statistics are delicate for a government litigant (France banned them in 2019), so any official use would be decided with Legal Services. Some source data carries non-commercial licence terms that would need confirming before any deployment.
Two sensitivities I’m keeping in view.
The hard part is done: new intelligence can now be built on top

Most of the effort so far has gone into the base layers: collecting the data, keeping the originals, reading decisions and dockets into structured facts, and linking decisions, files and citations to each other. With those in place, new features are mostly a matter of asking new questions of data that already exists.
Motion types, stage-aware file tracking and challenged-decision analysis were each added in days, because the docket data and the tests underneath were already there.

Time from filing to leave decision by year and registry, stay success rates by type of removal, how often files are discontinued, and caseload trends by decision-maker. All can be derived from what is stored.
Checking the Division’s own drafts against the case law, and summarizing how courts have handled each argument, once a capable model can run in-house.
“Within reach” items are not built yet. They are listed because the data they need is already in place.
Staying outside government is what lets it move this fast
Because iLit uses public information only, it doesn’t yet need approved hosting, a security assessment or a procurement process. That buys two things a departmental project rarely gets early on.
I can try an idea, test it on real data, and drop it the same week if it doesn’t work. Features like docket tracking, citation trends and paragraph meaning came out of that kind of trial and error.

Changes go from idea to working code in days, not quarters. More than 230 tasks have been recorded since early September; in the last two days alone the docket reader learned which steps apply at each stage of a file.

The trade-off is clear: it runs on my computer, it can’t touch internal documents, and nobody has vouched for it yet. Bringing it inside the department makes sense once it has proven itself, not before.
What comparable tools cost, and what this has cost

The Division has CanLII, which is free. Commercial platforms cost six figures a year and still don’t do what iLit does. Hiring out a build like this would take a funded team, a procurement cycle and many months.

What a little money would buy

This isn’t a formal request. The project keeps going either way. Funding decides two things: how fast it moves over the next few months, and whether its AI can move onto a machine that could one day sit inside the department and read internal material.
Why hardware is the real bottleneck
Only an AI model that runs on a machine under the department’s control can ever be allowed to read internal documents. How good that model can be depends almost entirely on the machine’s memory.

Is this a chatbot giving legal answers?
No. The core is rule-based and repeatable, and every answer points to its source. AI only adds labels that are checked and kept separate. It is a research aid, not legal advice.

They would add general research, sold per user, but none of them tracks Federal Court files, codes Minister outcomes, or analyses immigration citation trends. iLit does, at the cost of a machine and some AI services.
Why not just buy Westlaw or Lexis?
Could it read the Division’s internal documents?
Not with a public AI, and it doesn’t today. With local hardware the AI runs inside the department, so internal documents can be analysed without leaving it, once that use is authorized.

In samples of up to 100 decisions, every recorded citation position matched the source text exactly. Automated AI reviews of about 480 decisions flagged 70–81% fewer citation problems after fixes. Neither is a human accuracy check. A hand-reviewed accuracy check of file tracking and outcomes is one of my next steps.
It is a personal project, built on my own time with public data. If it were ever brought into the department, ownership and support would be settled then.
It isn’t ready, and staying outside keeps it flexible and fast. It makes more sense to prove its value first, then look at hosting, security and internal documents.
Why not bring it into government now?

Decisions are divided into evidence-sized text chunks.

The library currently contains searchable chunks. Each chunk belongs to a case and records its chunk set, position, label, paragraph range, text, text hash, and token estimate. Chunks are the units used for full-text search, semantic retrieval, citation evidence, and passage-level reading.

Because citation records connect source cases to cited authorities, the site can expose incoming and outgoing citation relationships, authority use over time, citation evidence, related decisions, and unresolved-reference quality checks. The graph is built from the underlying records, not from a manually curated list.

The platform is intentionally layered: raw intake, normalized case text, evidence extraction, derived analytics.

Raw source documents feed the ingestion pipeline. The pipeline creates or updates cases, case sources, and case chunks. Then evidence extraction creates citations, statute references, and tags. Derived layers such as judge profiles, citation metrics, outcome summaries, and FC procedural history are produced afterward and remain linkable back to the originating case text and source record.
The site is designed around a few concrete legal-research workflows, each powered by clean data and traceable provenance.

Normalized resolution then tries to map the citation string to a known target case, judge, or statute reference. This is done by matching raw text to normalized authority forms and by storing both the raw value and the resolved value in the same record. For example, a citation may appear as a full-case reference in one place and a statutory section-style reference elsewhere, but both remain linked to the source text and preserved separately.
Two kinds of values live in the system: source-grounded fields and analytical inferences.

. If a field is directly supported by a case record or a docket entry, it is treated as a strong extraction. If it is created by normalization or classification, it is labeled as a derived view and kept open to review.
In practice, we are careful to separate

is created after extraction and normalization. This includes decision outcomes, government outcome labels, judge profile alignment, judge win rates, citation centrality, authority use summaries, and trend lines. These are useful for research and pattern detection, but they are analytical outputs and should be read as summaries rather than direct quotations from the underlying source.

is taken directly from the source record or source metadata. This includes case title, court, date, docket, source URL, raw citation text, chunk text, statute reference text, recorded entry text, and the actual decision text. These fields are the most reliable because they can be traced back to the original source document or source intake record.
Win-rate and outcome analytics are derived from normalized metadata, not from direct quote extraction alone.

The platform is strong on explicit case metadata and statutory references. It is moderate for normalized outcome summaries and judge comparisons, especially where those values rely on repeated, consistent evidence. It is still an active improvement area for highly contextual legal conclusions, where the product should be treated as a research aid rather than a final legal conclusion.

are built by classifying the extracted metadata and decision processing results into a common outcome taxonomy. This makes aggregation across years, courts, and judges possible. The method is strongest when the decision clearly records a result or contains a well-structured outcome label. It is more approximate when the ruling is mixed, procedural, or only indirectly stated.
Where the current system is genuinely strong.

: cases remain tied to source text, chunks preserve location data, citations retain raw and normalized forms, and statutory references keep their source context. This gives the site a useful research workflow: search a case, inspect the decision text, open citation evidence, and trace the authority or statute back to the exact record from which it came.

We are also good at broad pattern detection. Repeated use of authorities, citation clustering, court-level patterns, and judge-level outcome aggregation all become visible once the underlying records are normalized. These are valuable for legal research because they help identify where arguments and authorities recur, even when the underlying dataset is still uneven.

19 / What does not work as well yet

The product is strongest as a research and triage platform. It is not yet a trusted autonomous legal reasoner. The design is intentionally honest about that: extracted facts stay visible, derived fields stay labeled, and the system keeps a clear path back to the original textual evidence.

Use of citations and outcomes is still not perfect. Some references are unresolved or ambiguous. Some authority patterns depend on weak or partial metadata. Some statute captures are narrow by design and intentionally conservative. Some judge-based or outcome-based summaries are only as good as the consistency of the underlying metadata and the quality of the normalization rules.

The search results, judged outcome summaries, citation intelligence dashboards, and FC timeline views are all produced by querying live tables and combining them.
